name: Mathematics Advanced
note: Core Mathematics Advanced facts and methods that both the current syllabus and the new one (first HSC exam 2027) use. Check with your teacher for anything your course adds or drops.

cards.f: What makes a relation a function?
cards.b: Each x-value (input) gives exactly one y-value (output). On a graph, every vertical line crosses it at most once.

cards.f: Define: domain and range.
cards.b: Domain: all the x-values a function can take. Range: all the y-values it produces.

cards.f: Domain of f(x) = sqrt(x − 3)?
cards.b: x ≥ 3, because the expression under a square root cannot be negative.

cards.f: Domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 2)?
cards.b: All real x except x = 2, because you cannot divide by zero.

cards.f: Test for an even function, and what its graph looks like.
cards.b: f(−x) = f(x) for all x. The graph is symmetric about the y-axis, e.g. y = x^2, y = cos x.

cards.f: Test for an odd function, and what its graph looks like.
cards.b: f(−x) = −f(x) for all x. The graph has point symmetry about the origin, e.g. y = x^3, y = sin x.

cards.f: What is a composite function f(g(x))?
cards.b: Apply g first, then apply f to the result. Its domain is the x-values in the domain of g whose outputs g(x) are in the domain of f.

cards.f: Gradient formula between (x1, y1) and (x2, y2).
Point-gradient form of a straight line.
Conditions for parallel and perpendicular lines.
cards.b: Parallel: m1 = m2. Perpendicular: m1 × m2 = −1.

cards.f: Quadratic formula and the discriminant.
cards.b: x = (−b ± sqrt(b^2 − 4ac)) / 2a. Δ = b^2 − 4ac: Δ > 0 two real roots, Δ = 0 one (repeated) root, Δ < 0 no real roots.

cards.f: Axis of symmetry and vertex of y = ax^2 + bx + c.
cards.b: Axis x = −b / 2a. Substitute that x to get the y-value of the vertex.

cards.f: Sum and product of the roots of ax^2 + bx + c = 0.
cards.b: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.

cards.f: What does y = f(x) + k do to the graph?
cards.b: Translates it k units up (down if k is negative).

cards.f: What does y = f(x − h) do to the graph?
cards.b: Translates it h units to the RIGHT (left if h is negative).

cards.f: What does y = a f(x) do to the graph?
cards.b: Dilates it vertically by a factor of a (stretches away from the x-axis). If a is negative it also reflects in the x-axis.

cards.f: What does y = f(bx) do to the graph?
cards.b: Dilates it horizontally by a factor of 1/b (towards the y-axis when b > 1). If b is negative it also reflects in the y-axis.

cards.f: y = k f(a(x + b)) + c: what order do you apply the changes?
cards.b: Horizontal: dilate by 1/a then translate b left. Vertical: dilate by k then translate c up. A safe check is to transform a few key points.

cards.f: How do you get y = −f(x) and y = f(−x) from y = f(x)?
cards.b: −f(x): reflect in the x-axis. f(−x): reflect in the y-axis.

cards.f: How do you solve f(x) = k graphically?
cards.b: Draw y = f(x) and the horizontal line y = k. The x-values where they meet are the solutions; count intersections to count solutions.

cards.f: Equation of a circle with centre (h, k) and radius r.
cards.b: (x − h)^2 + (y − k)^2 = r^2. Complete the square on x and y to find the centre and radius.

cards.f: What is the graph of y = |x|, and how do you solve |x − a| = b?
cards.b: A V shape with its vertex at the origin. |x − a| = b gives x − a = b or x − a = −b, so x = a ± b (needs b ≥ 0).

cards.f: What is an asymptote? Asymptotes of y = 1/(x − 2) + 3?
cards.b: A line the graph approaches but never reaches. Vertical x = 2, horizontal y = 3.

cards.f: How do you find the inverse of a function?
cards.b: Swap x and y, then make y the subject. The graph of the inverse is the reflection of the original in y = x.

cards.f: When does a function have an inverse function?
cards.b: When it is one-to-one (passes the horizontal line test). Otherwise restrict its domain first.

cards.f: How do you solve an inequality like x^2 − x − 6 < 0?
cards.b: Factorise: (x − 3)(x + 2) < 0. Sketch the parabola: it is below the x-axis between the roots, so −2 < x < 3.

cards.f: SOH CAH TOA.
cards.b: sin θ = opposite/hypotenuse, cos θ = adjacent/hypotenuse, tan θ = opposite/adjacent.

cards.f: Sine rule.
cards.b: a/sin A = b/sin B = c/sin C. Use it with a matching side and angle pair.

cards.f: Cosine rule (both forms).
cards.b: c^2 = a^2 + b^2 − 2ab cos C, and cos C = (a^2 + b^2 − c^2) / 2ab. Use it for two sides and the included angle, or all three sides.

cards.f: Area of a triangle using sine.
cards.b: A = ½ ab sin C, where C is the angle between sides a and b.

cards.f: What is the ambiguous case of the sine rule?
cards.b: Finding an angle with the sine rule can give two answers, θ and 180° − θ, when the given angle is opposite the shorter given side. Check both.

cards.f: Convert between degrees and radians.
cards.b: π radians = 180°. Degrees to radians: × π/180. Radians to degrees: × 180/π.

cards.f: Arc length and sector area (θ in radians).
cards.b: l = rθ and A = ½ r^2 θ.

cards.f: Exact values: sin, cos, tan of π/6 (30°).
cards.b: sin = 1/2, cos = sqrt(3)/2, tan = 1/sqrt(3).

cards.f: Exact values: sin, cos, tan of π/4 (45°).
cards.b: sin = 1/sqrt(2), cos = 1/sqrt(2), tan = 1.

cards.f: Exact values: sin, cos, tan of π/3 (60°).
cards.b: sin = sqrt(3)/2, cos = 1/2, tan = sqrt(3).

cards.f: ASTC: which ratios are positive in each quadrant?
cards.b: Q1 All, Q2 Sin, Q3 Tan, Q4 Cos (anticlockwise from the positive x-axis).

cards.f: Pythagorean identity.
cards.b: sin^2 θ + cos^2 θ = 1. Dividing through gives 1 + tan^2 θ = sec^2 θ and 1 + cot^2 θ = cosec^2 θ.

cards.f: Define sec, cosec and cot.
cards.b: sec θ = 1/cos θ, cosec θ = 1/sin θ, cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ / sin θ.

cards.f: Complementary angle results.
cards.b: sin(90° − θ) = cos θ and cos(90° − θ) = sin θ.

cards.f: Amplitude and period of y = a sin(bx) and y = a cos(bx).
cards.b: Amplitude |a|. Period 2π/b.

cards.f: Period of y = tan(bx).
cards.b: π/b. It has vertical asymptotes where cos(bx) = 0.

cards.f: y = a sin(b(x − h)) + k: what do h and k do?
cards.b: h is the phase shift (h units right). k moves the centre line to y = k.

cards.f: How do you solve sin x = 1/2 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
cards.b: Related angle π/6. Sine is positive in Q1 and Q2, so x = π/6 and x = π − π/6 = 5π/6.

cards.f: How do you solve sin 2x = k for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2π?
cards.b: Let u = 2x, so 0 ≤ u ≤ 4π. Find every u in that range, then halve each one.

cards.f: What is a bearing and how is it written?
cards.b: A direction measured clockwise from north, written as three digits, e.g. 060° or 235°.

cards.f: Angle of elevation versus depression.
cards.b: Elevation: measured up from the horizontal. Depression: measured down from the horizontal. They are equal as alternate angles.

cards.f: Index laws.
cards.b: a^m × a^n = a^(m+n), a^m ÷ a^n = a^(m−n), (a^m)^n = a^(mn), a^0 = 1, a^(−n) = 1/a^n, a^(1/n) = nth root of a.

cards.f: Definition of a logarithm.
cards.b: y = log_a x means a^y = x (a > 0, a ≠ 1, x > 0).

cards.f: Log laws.
cards.b: log(xy) = log x + log y, log(x/y) = log x − log y, log(x^n) = n log x, log_a a = 1, log_a 1 = 0.

cards.f: Change of base formula.
cards.b: log_a x = log_b x / log_b a, e.g. log_2 7 = ln 7 / ln 2.

cards.f: What is ln x?
cards.b: The natural logarithm: log base e, where e ≈ 2.71828. ln(e^x) = x and e^(ln x) = x.

cards.f: How do you solve 3^x = 20?
cards.b: Take logs of both sides: x ln 3 = ln 20, so x = ln 20 / ln 3 ≈ 2.73.

cards.f: How do you solve e^(2x) − 5e^x + 6 = 0?
cards.b: Let u = e^x: u^2 − 5u + 6 = 0, so u = 2 or 3. Then e^x = 2 or 3, so x = ln 2 or ln 3.

cards.f: Key features of y = e^x.
cards.b: Passes through (0, 1), always positive, increasing, horizontal asymptote y = 0, gradient at any point equals its y-value.

cards.f: Key features of y = ln x.
cards.b: Domain x > 0, passes through (1, 0), increasing, vertical asymptote x = 0. It is the reflection of y = e^x in y = x.

cards.f: Exponential growth and decay model.
cards.b: N = N0 e^(kt). k > 0 is growth, k < 0 is decay. N0 is the amount at t = 0.

cards.f: How do you find k if a population doubles in 5 years?
What does dN/dt = kN mean?
cards.b: The rate of change is proportional to the amount present. Its solution is N = N0 e^(kt).

cards.f: Define the derivative from first principles.
cards.b: f'(x) = limit as h → 0 of [f(x + h) − f(x)] / h.

cards.f: Derivative of x^n.
cards.b: n x^(n−1). Works for any real n, e.g. d/dx sqrt(x) = 1/(2 sqrt(x)).

cards.f: Chain rule.
cards.b: dy/dx = dy/du × du/dx. For y = [f(x)]^n: dy/dx = n[f(x)]^(n−1) f'(x).

cards.f: Product rule.
cards.b: d/dx (uv) = u'v + uv'.

cards.f: Quotient rule.
cards.b: d/dx (u/v) = (u'v − uv') / v^2.

cards.f: Derivatives of e^x and e^(f(x)).
cards.b: d/dx e^x = e^x. d/dx e^(f(x)) = f'(x) e^(f(x)).

cards.f: Derivatives of ln x and ln f(x).
cards.b: d/dx ln x = 1/x. d/dx ln f(x) = f'(x) / f(x).

cards.f: Derivative of a^x.
cards.b: a^x ln a.

cards.f: Derivatives of sin x, cos x and tan x (x in radians).
cards.b: sin x → cos x, cos x → −sin x, tan x → sec^2 x.

cards.f: Derivative of sin(ax + b).
cards.b: a cos(ax + b).

cards.f: How do you find the equation of a tangent at x = a?
cards.b: Gradient m = f'(a). Point (a, f(a)). Use y − f(a) = m(x − a).

cards.f: Gradient of the normal to a curve.
cards.b: The negative reciprocal of the tangent's gradient: −1/f'(a).

cards.f: What is a stationary point?
cards.b: A point where f'(x) = 0. It can be a local maximum, local minimum or a horizontal point of inflection.

cards.f: How do you tell a maximum from a minimum with the second derivative?
cards.b: At a stationary point: f''(x) < 0 means a maximum, f''(x) > 0 a minimum. If f''(x) = 0, test the gradient either side.

cards.f: What is a point of inflection?
cards.b: Where the concavity changes. f''(x) = 0 there AND f''(x) changes sign either side of it.

cards.f: Concave up versus concave down.
cards.b: Concave up: f''(x) > 0 (holds water, gradient increasing). Concave down: f''(x) < 0 (gradient decreasing).

cards.f: Steps for an optimisation question.
cards.b: Write the quantity in one variable, differentiate, set it to 0, solve, show it is a max or min (second derivative or table), check endpoints, answer in context.

cards.f: When is a function increasing or decreasing?
cards.b: Increasing where f'(x) > 0, decreasing where f'(x) < 0.

cards.f: How do displacement, velocity and acceleration connect?
cards.b: v = dx/dt and a = dv/dt = d^2x/dt^2. Going back: integrate a to get v, and v to get x.

cards.f: When is a particle at rest, and when is it speeding up?
cards.b: At rest when v = 0. Speeding up when v and a have the same sign.

cards.f: Distance travelled versus displacement.
cards.b: Displacement is final minus initial position. Distance adds up every movement, so split at each time v = 0.

cards.f: Integral of x^n.
Integral of (ax + b)^n.
Integrals of e^x and e^(ax+b).
cards.b: ∫ e^x dx = e^x + C. ∫ e^(ax+b) dx = (1/a) e^(ax+b) + C.

cards.f: Integral of 1/x and f'(x)/f(x).
cards.b: ∫ 1/x dx = ln|x| + C. ∫ f'(x)/f(x) dx = ln|f(x)| + C.

cards.f: Integrals of sin(ax) and cos(ax).
cards.b: ∫ sin(ax) dx = −(1/a) cos(ax) + C. ∫ cos(ax) dx = (1/a) sin(ax) + C.

cards.f: Integral of sec^2(ax).
cards.b: (1/a) tan(ax) + C.

cards.f: Integral of f'(x)[f(x)]^n.
cards.b: [f(x)]^(n+1) / (n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1 (reverse chain rule).

cards.f: Fundamental theorem of calculus.
cards.b: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a), where F is any antiderivative of f.

cards.f: Area when a curve goes below the x-axis.
cards.b: The integral is negative there. Split at the x-intercepts and add the absolute values of each part.

cards.f: Area between two curves.
cards.b: ∫ from a to b of [top curve − bottom curve] dx, where a and b are the intersection x-values.

cards.f: Trapezoidal rule.
cards.b: ∫ from a to b f(x) dx ≈ (h/2)[f(x0) + 2f(x1) + … + 2f(x(n−1)) + f(xn)], where h = (b − a)/n.

cards.f: Does the trapezoidal rule over- or under-estimate?
cards.b: Concave up: overestimate (trapezoids sit above the curve). Concave down: underestimate.

cards.f: How do you find the constant C in an integral?
cards.b: Substitute a known point (an initial condition) into the integrated equation and solve for C.

cards.f: Odd function integrated from −a to a?
cards.b: Zero. The areas above and below cancel.

cards.f: Arithmetic sequence: nth term.
cards.b: Tn = a + (n − 1)d, where a is the first term and d the common difference.

cards.f: Arithmetic series: sum of n terms (two forms).
cards.b: Sn = n/2 [2a + (n − 1)d], or Sn = n/2 (a + l) where l is the last term.

cards.f: Geometric sequence: nth term.
cards.b: Tn = a r^(n−1), where r is the common ratio.

cards.f: Geometric series: sum of n terms.
cards.b: Sn = a(r^n − 1)/(r − 1), or a(1 − r^n)/(1 − r). Use whichever keeps the denominator positive.

cards.f: Limiting sum of a geometric series and when it exists.
cards.b: S = a/(1 − r), only when −1 < r < 1.

cards.f: How do you test whether a sequence is arithmetic or geometric?
cards.b: Arithmetic: T2 − T1 = T3 − T2 (constant difference). Geometric: T2/T1 = T3/T2 (constant ratio).

cards.f: Compound interest formula.
cards.b: A = P(1 + r)^n, where r is the interest rate per period and n the number of periods.

cards.f: How do you adjust r and n for monthly compounding?
cards.b: Divide the annual rate by 12 and multiply the years by 12, e.g. 6% p.a. for 5 years: r = 0.005, n = 60.

cards.f: What is an annuity?
cards.b: A series of equal payments made at regular intervals, earning compound interest, e.g. regular savings or loan repayments.

cards.f: How do you use a future value interest factor table?
cards.b: FV = payment × table factor for the right rate per period and number of periods.

cards.f: How do you use a present value interest factor table?
cards.b: PV = payment × table factor. A loan's amount borrowed is the present value of its repayments.

cards.f: Steps for a reducing-balance loan question.
cards.b: Write A1, A2, A3 using A(n) = A(n−1)(1 + r) − M, spot the geometric series, sum it, then set An = 0 to find M or n.

cards.f: Why do loan repayments always reduce the balance by less at the start?
cards.b: Early on most of each repayment covers interest on a large balance, so little goes to the principal.

cards.f: Depreciation: straight line versus declining balance.
cards.b: Straight line: S = V0 − Dn (arithmetic). Declining balance: S = V0(1 − r)^n (geometric).

cards.f: Probability of A or B.
cards.b: P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B). If A and B are mutually exclusive, P(A ∩ B) = 0.

cards.f: Conditional probability.
cards.b: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

cards.f: Test for independent events.
cards.b: A and B are independent if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B), equivalently P(A | B) = P(A).

cards.f: Complementary events.
cards.b: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). 'At least one' questions are usually 1 − P(none).

cards.f: Discrete random variable: expected value.
cards.b: E(X) = Σ x P(X = x). It is the long-run mean.

cards.f: Discrete random variable: variance.
cards.b: Var(X) = E(X^2) − [E(X)]^2, where E(X^2) = Σ x^2 P(X = x). Standard deviation = sqrt(Var(X)).

cards.f: Conditions for a valid probability distribution.
cards.b: Every P(X = x) is between 0 and 1, and they add to 1.

cards.f: Effect of Y = aX + b on mean and variance.
cards.b: E(Y) = aE(X) + b. Var(Y) = a^2 Var(X). Adding b shifts the mean but not the spread.

cards.f: Conditions for a probability density function f(x).
cards.b: f(x) ≥ 0 for all x, and the total area under it is 1: ∫ f(x) dx = 1 over its domain.

cards.f: How do you find P(a ≤ X ≤ b) for a continuous random variable?
cards.b: ∫ from a to b of f(x) dx (the area under the pdf). For continuous variables P(X = a) = 0.

cards.f: What is the cumulative distribution function F(x)?
cards.b: F(x) = P(X ≤ x) = ∫ from the lower end up to x of f(t) dt. It rises from 0 to 1.

cards.f: How do you find the median of a continuous distribution?
cards.b: Solve F(m) = 0.5, i.e. the area under the pdf up to m equals 1/2.

cards.f: Define a z-score and what it tells you.
cards.b: z = (x − μ)/σ. The number of standard deviations a value is above (positive) or below (negative) the mean.

cards.f: Empirical rule for a normal distribution.
cards.b: About 68% within 1 SD of the mean, 95% within 2 SD, 99.7% within 3 SD.

cards.f: How do you compare scores from two different tests?
cards.b: Convert each to a z-score. The higher z-score is the better relative performance.

cards.f: Bivariate data: what does Pearson's r measure?
cards.b: The strength and direction of a LINEAR relationship, from −1 to 1. Near ±1 strong, near 0 weak or none.

cards.f: Describe r = −0.85.
cards.b: A strong negative linear correlation: as x increases, y tends to decrease.

cards.f: Interpolation versus extrapolation.
cards.b: Interpolation predicts inside the data range (reliable). Extrapolation predicts outside it (less reliable).

cards.f: How do you interpret the gradient of a least-squares regression line?
cards.b: For each 1 unit increase in x, y changes by the gradient on average, e.g. y = 29.2 − 0.011x: each extra metre lowers y by 0.011.

cards.f: Does strong correlation prove causation?
cards.b: No. A third factor or coincidence can link the two variables.

cards.f: What is the interquartile range and how are outliers found?
cards.b: IQR = Q3 − Q1. Outliers lie below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR.

cards.f: Effect of an outlier on the mean and median.
cards.b: It pulls the mean towards it. The median barely changes, so use the median for skewed data.

cards.f: Positive versus negative skew.
cards.b: Positively skewed: tail to the right, mean > median. Negatively skewed: tail to the left, mean < median.
